terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “particular, peculiar, especial (opp. communis)”: more than others get, or more than usual. The adverb praecipuē is “especially” (see particular).

evidence: Cic. Imp. Pomp. 3: singulāris eximiaque virtūs (Lewis & Short)
Cic. Off. 1.67: ea quae eximia plērīsque et praeclāra videntur (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: “Taken out” of the mass (eximō, Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: special to, peculiar to, one’s own
evidence: Ov. Met. 6.350: nec sōlem proprium nātūra … fēcit
Traupman 162: proprium ingenium, a special talent
terms.comment: What belongs to one person or thing and not to others.

evidence: Traupman 130: pretium speciāle, a special offer
terms.comment: A term of logic and rhetoric, opposed to generālis, and post-Augustan (Lewis & Short); it does not mean “out of the ordinary”. Traupman’s pretium speciāle (see bargain) is a modern use.

phrases.latin: ingeneratque in prīmīs praecipuum quendam amōrem in eōs quī prōcreātī sunt
phrases.english: and above all nature implants a special love for those one has brought into the world

phrases.latin: praeter Aeduōs et Rēmōs, quōs praecipuō semper honōre Caesar habuit
phrases.english: except the Aedui and the Remi, whom Caesar always held in special honour

caesar.html: Lewis & Short cites the passage as Caes. BG 5.52; the Perseus text has it at 5.54.4.

sources: Lewis & Short: praecipuus · Lewis & Short: singularis · Lewis & Short: eximius · Lewis & Short: proprius · Lewis & Short: specialis
